# SPOS Net — full documentation for AI crawlers

SPOS Net (https://spos-systems.github.io/SPOS-Net/) is a free and open-source internet speed test, available in Arabic (right-to-left) and English, developed by SPOS — صولة للأنظمة (https://spos.ly) and released under the MIT license (source: https://github.com/spos-systems/SPOS-Net).

## What it measures

1. **Download speed (Mbps)** — Measured with parallel HTTP GET streams (50 MiB chunks from `speed.cloudflare.com/__down`, plus a self-hosted 16 MB incompressible file mirrored on jsDelivr and raw.githubusercontent) spread across up to 9 independent TCP connections: Cloudflare on HTTPS ports 443/2053/2083/2087/2096/8443 (each port a separate origin) plus the static mirrors — so a single congested connection cannot cap the result even when an ISP filters the alternate ports. The measurement clock starts at the first received byte; the TCP ramp-up window (at least 1.5 s or 18% of the phase) is excluded. The final figure follows Speedtest.net's documented methodology: instantaneous samples over the stable window are sorted, the two fastest are removed, the slowest ~22% are discarded, and the mean of the remainder is reported — the same way speedtest.net computes its headline number. A sustained average and a peak (best 500 ms window) are also reported. Live values use a rolling 1-second window.
2. **Upload speed (Mbps)** — Measured with parallel XHR POST streams of random bytes carrying real-time `upload.onprogress` events, so bytes are counted the moment they are sent rather than when a request completes, with the same Speedtest-style trimmed mean as the final figure. Chunk size adapts to the observed speed (512 KiB – 16 MiB, starting at 4 MiB). Connections are warmed during the latency phase and spread across up to 4 ports; in-flight requests are aborted exactly at the deadline. Same ramp exclusion and windowing as download.
3. **Latency / ping (ms)** — Time-to-first-byte of empty (0-byte) requests, after a warm-up request. Twelve samples produce min, median, average and max. The median is shown as the headline ping.
4. **Jitter (ms)** — Mean absolute difference between consecutive latency samples (RFC 3550-style inter-arrival variation, applied to HTTP RTT).
5. **Estimated packet loss (%)** — A burst of 24 short timed requests (concurrency 6, timeout 2.8 s); the share of failed/timed-out requests approximates loss at the HTTP level. This is an estimate: browsers cannot emit ICMP, and TCP retransmissions are invisible to JavaScript.
6. **Latency under load (ms)** — Additional 0-byte probes issued every ~0.9 s while download and upload streams saturate the line; the gap versus idle latency is graded A+ (≤5 ms), A (≤30 ms), B (≤60 ms), C (≤150 ms), D (≤300 ms) or F (>300 ms) as a bufferbloat indicator.
7. **Live speed graph** — Instant throughput (rolling 1-second window) is plotted in real time on a canvas strip under the gauge: download in blue, upload in violet, with a dashed divider between phases.
8. **Download consistency** — Average-to-peak ratio of the download phase; low values indicate an unstable line.

## Professional options

- Display unit: Mbps (default), MB/s, or kbps — applies to gauge, tiles and exports.
- Phase duration: 8 s (quick), 12 s (standard), 20 s (thorough) for download and upload.
- Parallel streams: 1 / 4 / 8 / 16, spread across all independent connections (Cloudflare ports + static mirrors).
- Toggles: latency-under-load sampling, packet-loss burst test.
- Share: share as an image card straight into the phone's share sheet (Web Share API Level 2 file sharing, with PNG download fallback), copy a result link (result encoded in the URL fragment — nothing is stored server-side), copy a text summary, save a 1200×630 PNG result card, export JSON, share via WhatsApp / X / Telegram, or use the native OS share sheet where available.
- Result ID: every run gets a short identifier (e.g. SP-4F9K2Q1) derived from the result itself, shown in the details drawer, on the image card and in shared links.
- Real-world estimates: time to download a 1 GB file, a 10 GB game and a 7 GB 4K movie, and to upload 500 MB of photos — computed from the measured speeds.
- Connection details: public IP, ASN and ISP name, city/country, Cloudflare colo serving the test, HTTP protocol version, and the measurement method (streams × TCP connections).
- Connection score: 0–100 weighted score (download 42%, upload 23%, ping 20%, jitter 8%, loss 7%) with a grade, a one-line verdict and usage-suitability badges: 4K streaming (≥25 Mbps), HD streaming (≥5 Mbps), HD video calls, competitive gaming (ping ≤60 ms, jitter ≤15 ms, loss <1%), casual gaming (ping ≤120 ms), large downloads (≥100 Mbps). Ping, jitter and loss tiles are tinted green/amber/red by quality thresholds after each run.
- Test history: last 20 runs kept in the browser's localStorage only.
- Keyboard shortcuts: Space (start/stop), S (settings), D (details).
- URL parameters: `?lang=ar|en` forces a language; `?auto=1` starts the test automatically on load (useful for kiosks and embeds). On first visit the app follows the browser language automatically.
- Installable PWA: the service worker precaches the app shell (HTML, CSS, JS, icons, logo) so the app opens instantly and works offline after the first visit; the install button appears when the browser exposes `beforeinstallprompt`, and iOS Safari users get an “Add to Home Screen” guide.

## Privacy and architecture

- Fully static site (HTML/CSS/JS, zero dependencies, no build step) hosted on GitHub Pages.
- All measurements run in the visitor's browser against public Cloudflare endpoints: `speed.cloudflare.com/__down?bytes=N`, `speed.cloudflare.com/__up`, `speed.cloudflare.com/meta`. These endpoints are used by Cloudflare's own speed test and send CORS headers allowing third-party use.
- No accounts, ads, analytics or server-side logging. ASN organization names are optionally resolved through RIPEstat (`stat.ripe.net`) when the meta endpoint omits them.
- Test history and settings never leave the browser.

## Common questions

- **Is it accurate?** Browser-based tests measure HTTP throughput, the same class of measurement as other web speed tests (Cloudflare, Fast.com). SPOS Net spreads streams across up to 6 independent TCP connections — the same multi-connection model used by leading desktop test apps — so a lossy or long path cannot cap the result at a single connection's congestion window. Single-stream mode approximates one large file download.
- **Why do different apps show different numbers?** Servers and paths differ: an ISP-local test server gives a shorter path and higher numbers, while a global anycast edge measures a realistic end-to-end path. Small differences (±10%) between any two tools are normal; large gaps usually mean one tool tests a shorter path or uses a different ramp-up/averaging method.
- **Why Cloudflare endpoints?** They are the only public, CORS-enabled, upload-capable measurement endpoints suitable for a dependency-free static site, and anycast routing automatically selects the nearest edge.
- **Why is packet loss "estimated"?** Browsers cannot send ICMP packets; the HTTP failure-rate burst is the closest observable proxy.
- **Cost?** Free, no ads, open source under MIT.
- **What is bufferbloat?** The rise in latency while the line is busy (downloads/uploads in progress) — a common cause of laggy calls and games during transfers. SPOS Net grades it A+…F from the latency increase measured under load.
